detail: p. 704, IV.C.i, second key point: Direction and any restriction must be demonstrated at all three sites as applicable. The revision restores the presence conditions but reduces the ductal and isthmic requirements to a generic flow assessment.
p. 712, AV Septal Defects: The crux finding compares closed leaflets and prompts assessment of the valve and septa.
p. 713, Fig. 23: The approximate 2:1 ratio is explicitly contingent on the index equation. The stated endpoint is anticipated palliation.
p. 712, General Imaging Approach: Colour assessment of AV regurgitation is supported here. The common-valve row on 706 provides lesion-specific context.
p. 712, AV Septal Defects: The listed causes of obstruction include the AV valve and accessory tissue as well as conal and subvalvular structures.
p. 712, General Imaging Approach: Redistribution can lower the peak velocity. The text distinguishes right-sided annular measurements from atrial shunting in left-sided obstruction.

p. 713, crisscross connections: Sidedness and morphologic concordance are now distinguished correctly. The positional drainage pattern described is usual, whereas the revised statement still presents it without that qualifier.
p. 713, crisscross connections: The association with VSD and straddling is now confined to discordance within the twisted connection.
p. 710, Table 14: The foramen ovale row includes d-TGA, HLHS, critical left obstruction and isolated restriction.
p. 711, Fig. 21: Panel C links the Doppler finding to moderately elevated pressure in this illustrated fetus. The three panels support the other features.
p. 715, IV.C.iii, first key point: Fetal echocardiography precedes counselling about prognosis, associations and further testing.
p. 715, IV.C.iii: The arch side must be recorded at least once. Delineating branching is an attempt, particularly for opposite-sided arches.
p. 707, Table 13: The revised grouping follows the TOF key-observations cell, including its separate three-vessel observation.
p. 707–708, Table 13: The observations are assigned to d-TGA. The separate l-TGA row is on the next page.
p. 714–715, Fig. 26: Panel E identifies the pulmonary artery by its branching. The surrounding examples include Taussig–Bing and l-TGA.
p. 715, IV.C.iii: Both four-chamber observations support possible recognition of l-TGA.
p. 714, DORV paragraph: Subpulmonary VSD, subaortic obstruction, associated coarctation and arch imaging with colour and 2D are discussed together in DORV.
p. 714, common arterial trunk paragraph: Complete ductal dependence for the lower body and prostaglandin at birth apply to the specified subsets.

p. 715, IV.C.iv, Progressive Lesions, Obstructive and Regurgitant, introductory paragraph above the semilunar obstruction subheading. This paragraph establishes progression risk and serial assessment for both categories.
p. 715, Semilunar Valve Obstruction with an Intact Ventricular Septum: Severe early obstruction can cause ventricular hypoplasia or hydrops when contralateral filling is compromised.

p. 715, IV.C.iv, Progressive Lesions, Obstructive and Regurgitant, introductory paragraph above the semilunar obstruction subheading. This is the shared source for the five vascular Doppler assessments with progression.
p. 708, Table 13, aortic stenosis: The ascending aortic enlargement is a possible finding (±). This symbol modifies the finding, not the imaging view.
p. 716, IV.C.iv: The interpretation of higher regurgitant velocities is conditional on more severe disease. The alternative explanations for low velocities are present.
p. 716 and 708, Table 13: The prose supplies the atresia/small RV context and to-and-fro signal. The table specifies the low-velocity colour setting.
p. 719, Table 15: HLHS with MR appears in the heart failure risk row. The 2–4 week interval is suggested at provider discretion.
p. 717, TV disease imaging: Vena contracta width relative to the annulus is given as one method of assessing TR severity.
p. 717, TV disease: The features refer to severe tricuspid valve disease, the lesion identified in this entry. Lack of augmentation and the investigational status are preserved.
p. 717, IV.C.v and 709, Table 13: The prose lists group-level warning signs. The table assigns the U-shaped view to vascular rings.
p. 718, IV.C.v, first key point: The upper mediastinal view is recommended in the arch-anatomy assessment.
p. 718, IV.C.v, second key point: An attempt to identify aberrant subclavian origin is particularly relevant with suspected abnormal arch laterality.
p. 2226, recommendation 2: Family history now specifies CHD. Both NT thresholds, abnormal ductus venosus condition and individual Class I evidence grades match.
p. 2226, recommendation 4: The relative is second degree with CHD. Exposure timing, anatomical indications and IIb evidence levels match.

p. 2226, recommendation 5: The isolated CHD population, HbA1c boundary and III grades match. The drug term is explicitly identified as printed. Preserve the editorial caveat concerning the different terminology in Table 2.
p. 2227, recommendation 13: Known and suspected conduction abnormalities, modality-specific indications, research status and IIa/B/C are supported.
p. 2227, recommendation 14: The population is known CHD. Counselling, an offer of testing and an anatomical survey are Class I/A.
p. 2227, recommendation 15: Brain and chest MRI are tied to the respective findings and purpose specified in IIa/B.
p. 2227, recommendation 16: Both the brain-screening population and the purpose of chest MRI match IIb/B.
p. 2227, recommendation 17: Known CHD and the third-trimester risk conditions for NST and BPP agree with IIb/C.
p. 2227, recommendation 19: The strict rate threshold, higher-rate alternatives and wording about considering therapy agree with IIa/B.
p. 2227, recommendation 20: The option to consider therapy applies to intermittent VT above 200 bpm (IIa/B).
p. 2227, recommendation 23: All four candidates and the intact ventricular septum in pulmonary atresia are correctly specified (IIb/B/C).

p. 2208, Extracardiac Abnormalities, Incidence: The two percentages and upper-end fetal qualifier match, but the infant and fetal cohorts have congenital heart disease. The revised statement still generalises to heart disease.
p. 2208, Fetal MRI: The uncertainty concerns extracardiac screening with known CHD and normal ultrasound.
p. 2208, Fetal Wellness Assessment, Rationale: The selected-risk indication, lack of targeted studies in isolated CHD and potential harms of false positives are present.
p. 2209, Biophysical Profile: The caution about widespread use pertains to selected at-risk CHD groups. Earlier delivery is an anticipated consequence.
p. 2209, Prenatal Counseling and Parental Stress: The four counselling aims, support and optional composition of the team are supported.
p. 2209, Essential Elements: Counselling is to be offered promptly, preferably on the day of the examination.
p. 2210, Techniques: The statement dates the evidence gap to its publication and specifies counselling after prenatal CHD diagnosis.
p. 2210, Techniques: Ongoing assessment of understanding, repeated sessions when needed and access to support during pregnancy match.
p. 2218, HLHS With Restrictive or Intact Atrial Septum: The severe outcomes apply to the highly restrictive or intact septum. Lesser restriction is distinguished.
p. 2222, Delivery Planning: The revised wording reports what the available studies showed and correctly dates the absence of randomised evidence in severe CHD.

p. 2224–2225, Foramen Ovale–Dependent Lesions: Tethering or bowing and the later study are introduced at the foot of 2224. The outcome and limitation continue below Table 20 on 2225. Include both pages.
p. 2226, Complex CHD With Heart Failure: Attribution of hydrops, gestational suitability, reversibility or treatability and preparation for immediate treatment are retained.
p. 2225, Table 20, d-TGA: The IIb/C action for pulmonary hypertension is tied to abnormal ductal flow. Small calibre is listed among abnormal findings.
